newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine 9-mth GNP growth seen at 7.16 pct -poll.
newsitem.headline: Philippine 9-mth GNP growth seen at 7.16 pct -poll.

text.p: The Philippines' gross national product (GNP) growth in the first nine months of the year is expected to reach 7.16 percent from 5.6 percent in the year-ago period, the average from a Reuter poll of analysts on Tuesday showed.
The growth would be fuelled by a rebound in the agricultural sector as well as robust investments, analysts said ahead of the official release of GNP figures next week.
Gross Domestic Product (GDP), which is GNP excluding income from overseas, was seen growing by 5.53 percent, an increase from 4.9 percent in the first nine months of 1995.
The government has set a 1996 GNP growth target of 7.5 percent to 8.5 percent against 5.7 percent in 1995.
"GNP (for nine months) can easily pierce the seven percent level," said Rolando Valenzuela, senior vice president at Philippine TA Securities.
"Relatively, all sectors are doing well," said Manny Lim, vice president of ING Bank. He predicted GNP growth would touch 7.0 percent to 7.5 percent in the nine-month period.
In the first half of this year, Philippine GNP grew by 7.06 percent against 5.6 percent in the year-ago period. GDP was at 5.05 percent versus the year-earlier 4.7 percent.
Analysts said a slowdown in export growth was the only setback, but they expected electronics, the country's leading export item, to rebound.
In the latest nine-month period, Philippine exports stood at $14.926 billion, marking a slower growth rate of 16.6 percent from 31.3 percent in the year-ago period.
Electronics comprised 42 percent of total exports while garments accounted for 15 percent.
Analysts said the electronics sector was hampered by a slowdown in world demand, while Philippine garments were outpriced by cheaper products from other countries.
The farm sector, which made up about 21 percent of the country's output, recovered by 4.17 percent in the first nine months due to better weather conditions after flat growth in the 1995 period.
The improvement of the sector had lowered inflation this year to an average of 9.1 percent for the latest 10-month period versus the year-earlier 9.7 percent.
That would also translate to an improvement in farm incomes that would lead to higher consumer spending, analysts said.
"The third quarter is usually the time for building of inventories," TA Securities' Valenzuela said, adding that this was in preparation for Christmas spending.

Analysts also said the stable foreign exchange rate, the government's budget surplus and healthy balance-of-payments position contributed to the country's strong growth. All of these together helped tame inflation.
Following were GNP and GDP forecasts made for the January to September period:
